solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

flags: minor: distractors A and C are clearly unsupported; D is the only real competitor (and is contradicted by the ending, where the narrator keeps translating and hides the change)
R036-01.notes: Para 5 ('for years I had never let him have it') plus the father's good-humored response together make B the central idea. D tempts readers who expect a 'resolution' but nothing says the family stops relying on the narrator.

flags: minor: key closely paraphrases 'taking the jolts out of every conversation before they reached the other side' (para 2), which makes it a near-lookup for careful readers
minor: overlaps conceptually with R036-01 and R036-04 (the softening habit is tested three times)
R036-02.notes: Both examples (gas company, pharmacist) show softening in both directions. C is the main trap ('Everyone stayed calm'), but conversations were not stopped. A misreads 'theft'.

flags: minor: B and C are throwaway choices; D is a literal-reading trap only
R036-03.notes: 'Asks for something he believes he has already paid for' = blunt and entitled, which matches the 'theft' remark in para 2.

flags: minor: answer is stated outright in para 5 ('It was not the sentence I had been given. It was the sentence I would have wanted to hear'), so this is a lookup
minor: A and D are implausible choices that almost nobody would pick; B has no support
R036-04.notes: The narrator hears a softened version and stops; para 5 explains why.

flags: Key's 'a role meant for an adult' is not established by the text: the teacher asked only for 'an interpreter', and the narrator's age at the conference is never given (only 'by the time I was twelve'; Tomas is nine). The key is the best choice but rests on an unstated inference. Consider rewording, e.g. 'stress that the role of interpreter fell, as usual, to the narrator.'
minor: B (resentment) gets some support from 'a second job that no one paid me for' and may draw students; the narrator's tone is matter-of-fact rather than resentful, though
R036-05.notes: The flat short sentence contrasts the teacher's formal request for 'an interpreter' with the family reality that the child does it. D is a misreading, since Ms. Pruitt asked for 'an interpreter', not the narrator. C has no support.

flags: minor: overlaps with R036-07 (both test the father's laugh and his reply in para 7)
R036-06.notes: The narrator 'braced for the sharpness'; 'Instead he laughed' and he thanked her. A and C contradict the text, and B is unsupported.

R036-07.notes: Tomas's behavior (interrupting, arguing, owning the conversation) mirrors the father's blunt manner from para 1. C ('smart') is a good trap for quick readers. D is a weak inference.

flags: minor: A ('immediately', from 'straight away') is the only plausible trap; B and D are filler
R036-08.notes: 'Telling him straight' = honestly, without softening, which ties to the theme.

flags: minor: 'quiet' does not map cleanly to 'slower, more careful translating'. The narrator was talking throughout, so students may hesitate, though A is clearly the best choice and the narrator's reply ('trying to get it right') confirms it
minor: D could draw readers who recall the narrator pausing after the father's laugh ('did not translate right away'), but the father did not laugh 'at Ms. Pruitt's remarks' in a mocking sense
R036-09.notes: Para 6 says the translation 'came out slower... with pauses where I would normally have smoothed'. The narrator's answer 'I had been trying to get it right' confirms A. B and C are unsupported.
